hooks.name: Logo, wordmark, symbol, lockups
hooks.ask: Do you have a logo? Which versions: symbol only, horizontal and stacked lockups, one-color?
hooks.accepts: Master SVG or PDF with text outlined (EPS legacy); derived transparent PNG in color, black and white
hooks.does: Places it in the app bar, sign-in and emails per the logo rules in DC-L05-13; proposes brand-color candidates from its fills; derives app icon, favicon and social image drafts
hooks.if_no: Commission a designer (brief + assignment reminder). AI logo generators (Looka, Brandmark) with caveats: Looka says its icons and fonts come from a shared database and stay available to others, and trademark filing needs an attorney; run a trademark search before adoption. Wordmark-only fallback: the brand name set in the chosen typeface (OFL, Google Fonts, Adobe Fonts and ITF FFL all allow fonts in logos)
hooks.checks: SVG parses; no `<text>` nodes; no embedded raster in the master; viewBox present; SVGO pass; one-fill mono variant; legibility at 16 and 32px; renders on light and dark surfaces

Q-brand-03.accepts: SVG (preferred, one master for the favicon set), PDF or EPS vector, or PNG at 512px or larger; light, dark and monochrome versions if they exist. The builder then derives `favicon.ico` 32px, `icon.svg` with a dark-scheme style, `apple-touch-icon.png` 180px, manifest PNGs 192 and 512 plus a maskable 512 [S-L05-042, S-L05-040, S-L05-041]

Skeletons (gray boxes) for page or area loads, spinners for smaller parts (Carbon skeletons only on containers) [S-L13-033, S-L05-071].
Spinner inside the button you pressed, which keeps focus (S2 pending after 1 s; Carbon inline loading) [S-L08-067, S-L08-061].

questions.ask: Should text boxes have a border or a shaded fill, and where should their labels go?

options.l: Fields with a border (M3 outlined; Carbon) [S-L08-105, S-L08-106].
Fields with a shaded fill (M3 filled) [S-L08-105].
Label always above, hint under the label [S-L13-066].
Hint text inside the box as the label
Mark only the rarer of required or optional, "(optional)" or "(required)" [S-L08-106].

questions.ask: When should a form check answers, and can the submit button ever be turned off?

options.l: On submit, a list of errors at the top that takes focus, "Error:" prefix, notes by each field (GOV.UK) [S-L08-077].
When you leave a field ("reward early, punish late")
Turn off submit on short forms until all is right, never on long ones (Carbon) [S-L08-106].
Never turn off submit; explain the problem instead (Atlassian) [S-L08-085].

questions.ask: Where should error messages show up, and how should they be worded?

options.l: Error next to the field it is about [DC-L13-07].
Error summary at the top of the form [DC-L13-07].
A pop-up box that blocks the page [DC-L13-07].
Full error page for catastrophic failures [DC-L13-07].

questions.ask: Where should messages like 'Saved' appear: in place, in a banner, or in a toast that fades?

options.l: Inline or banner by default; toasts only for low-stakes confirmations with undo, never auto-dismissing toasts that contain actions (Carbon matrix of 4 statuses x 7 types) [S-L08-079; DC-L13-09].
No toasts; banners and dialogs only (Primer) [S-L08-098, S-L08-012].
Toasts and flags used widely (M3 snackbar, Atlassian flags) [S-L08-008, S-L08-011].

questions.ask: When people delete something, should they get an undo button, an 'Are you sure?' step, or both?

options.l: Undo with trash or soft delete for actions you can reverse (NN/g calls undo superior; Shneiderman rule 6) [S-L13-067, S-L13-037].
An 'Are you sure?' box with clear verb buttons, and Cancel as the safe choice [S-L13-067; DC-L13-08].
Undo when it can be undone, ask first when it can't or costs a lot [DC-L13-08].

questions.ask: Which tasks should open in a box in the middle, a panel that slides in, or a small pop-up?

options.l: Block the page only if it clearly helps; panels and pop-ups for small tasks; full screen for big flows (HIG) [S-L08-086].
Panels that slide in from the bottom or side (M3, Fluent, Atlassian) [S-L08-008, S-L08-010, S-L08-011].

questions.ask: How should long lists load: in pages, with a 'Load more' button, or by scrolling on and on?

options.l: Infinite scroll, for feeds of same-kind items [S-L08-073].

questions.ask: Should people see every option at once, or the main ones first with the rest tucked away?

options.l: Main options first, extras behind a clearly named button, two levels at most [S-L13-063].
One step at a time (a wizard), only when steps stand alone [S-L13-063].
Show extras on hover or when something is picked [DC-L13-03].

questions.ask: What should an empty screen show, and how should first-time users learn the product?

options.l: Empty states for first use, user-cleared, no results, no permission or error (Primer Blankslate, Spectrum IllustratedMessage, shadcn Empty) [DC-L13-10; S-L08-012, S-L08-015, S-L08-018].
Tips and empty-screen hints right when people need them [S-L13-070].
A guided tour, only for truly new and complex screens [S-L13-070].

questions.ask: How firmly should we stop design tricks, like boxes ticked for you or a louder 'Yes' button?

options.l: A written ban on the 16 tricks at deceptive.design, like sneaking and fake urgency [S-L13-071].
Written down, and blocked where a tool can spot it

questions.ask: What one number or status should people see without opening the app?

options.l: One fact per complication, one or two per tile, alerts when urgent, all in the app (Google) [S-L14-015].
Complications, Smart Stack, Live Activities, CarPlay widgets [S-L14-001, S-L14-047].

questions.show_if: Q-plat-02 marks watch or car first-class, or the product ships widgets

questions.ask: Does your product use AI, and if so, how should people spot and fix its work?

options.l: An AI tag and an AI button (Carbon AI label; S2 genai; Atlassian Rovo) [S-L08-009, S-L08-067, S-L08-063].
An AI mode that normal parts can switch on
Chat components for products people talk to (shadcn Message, Bubble; Carbon AI chat) [S-L08-018, S-L14-058].

questions.ask: Should buttons and cards use raw colors and sizes, or go through layers of named values?

options.l: Two layers, raw then role, plus component tokens when needed (Atlassian, Polaris; Fluent global + alias) [S-L07-107, S-L07-125, S-L01-033].
Three layers for every part, raw, role, then part (Material 3; Primer base, functional, component) [S-L07-102, S-L01-027].

questions.ask: Should stored sizes be pixels, plain numbers, or rem (the web unit that grows with the browser's text size)?

options.l: px in source, rem on the web (DTCG allows px and rem only; Figma imports px) [S-L07-002, S-L07-011, S-L03-037].
Plain numbers in steps of 4, output 1:1 as pt, dp, epx or px; rem for web font sizes (Fluent's ramp) [S-L10-039].
rem in the source, turned into dp, sp or CGFloat by the build [DC-L10-08].

questions.ask: Which file format and build tool should turn your tokens into code for each platform?

options.l: DTCG 2025.10 + Resolver, one file per tier and mode (stable since 28 Oct 2025) [S-L07-002, S-L07-004].
Tokens Studio + sd-transforms, when designers author in the plugin [DC-L07-25].

questions.ask: What naming rules should tokens follow, so people and AI tools read them the same way?

options.l: Names in a fixed order, like ds.color.bg.accent.hover, for roles and parts [DC-L07-04].
Space steps named by percent of base (space.200 = 16px; Atlassian, Material), and role names [S-L03-003, S-L03-030].
A 2-4 letter prefix in code only (--ds-, --cds-, --md-); no theme or brand in names [S-L07-036, S-L07-108].
Lowercase JSON segments; kebab for CSS, camel for JS/Swift/Kotlin, snake for Android XML [S-L07-158].

questions.ask: Which kinds of values should get a token, from the basics up to almost all of them?

options.l: Plus corners, borders, shadows, opacity and motion [DC-L07-07].
Plus layer order (z-index), breakpoints, icon sizes, touch targets and chart colors [DC-L07-07; S-L07-036].

questions.ask: How should styles made of several values, like a text style or a shadow, be stored?
How should dark mode, contrast and density mix without too many versions to test?

options.l: Every mix in one flat list (the DTCG resolver example
Separate settings that never change the same tokens [DC-L07-17].
A Breakpoint collection (3 modes) for layout, and grid auto layout for parts with columns [DC-L07-28; S-L07-024].

questions.ask: How should the Figma library stay tidy, so designers pick the right values?

options.l: Hide raw values, and offer each variable only where its name fits [S-L07-018, S-L07-025].
Make Web, Android and iOS code names from the build's name rules [S-L07-018].
Variables for values, styles for bundles [S-L07-019].
Run Check designs before "Ready for dev" and review library analytics quarterly (Org/Enterprise; the builder lints on Professional) [S-L07-025, S-L07-029].

questions.ask: How should each token explain its use, and how should old tokens be phased out?

options.l: A short note ($description) on each semantic token [S-L07-002].
Check library analytics before you remove it (Org/Enterprise) [S-L07-029].

questions.ask: What should set the theme's look, and what may clients or other brands change?

options.l: One source color plus a scheme variant and contrast level (Material) [S-L06-082, S-L06-083].
An admin page, "clicks, not code", for colors, logos, images and chosen accents (Salesforce SLDS 2) [S-L06-068].
A theme builder for your users (Linear base, accent, contrast) [S-L06-012].
Overrides people edit in the CMS [S-L06-053].

questions.ask: How strict should the system be, and can product teams change it or add their own parts?

options.l: A strict core, plus team-owned add-ons, the "expanded universe" (Dan Mall) [S-L11-014].

questions.ask: In what order will you build the system, try it in one product, and roll it out?

options.l: Pick the pilot by 8 tests, like shared parts, a champion, a 3-4 week scope and few ties to old code [S-L11-105].
Roll out step by step, worst problems first; all at once only with a rebrand [S-L11-105].

questions.ask: Who can add to the system, and how will decisions be made and written down?

options.l: A fast lane for fixes, icons and docs; a proposal (RFC) lane for new components [S-L11-020, S-L11-021].
Brad Frost's 10-step flow, with a path for one-off needs [S-L11-003].
Decision records (ADRs) from day one, made from your answers here [S-L11-095; inferred].

questions.ask: How should you mark each component's status, number its versions, and retire old ones?

options.l: Experimental, then Ready, then Deprecated (Primer cut five to three) [S-L11-025, S-L11-026].
One SemVer for the whole library while small; one per package on many platforms [S-L11-106, S-L11-028].
A version number for each component (Atlassian, Paste) [S-L11-028].
Warn with @deprecated in a minor release, ship codemods, drop it in the next major (Polaris) [S-L11-100].

questions.ask: What problem hurts most today, and how will you measure whether the system helped?

options.l: Design use and code use (Figma analytics; a scanner like Omlet or react-scanner) [S-L11-035, S-L11-037, S-L11-039].
A survey every quarter on how happy people are with it [S-L11-030].

questions.ask: How will you tell people about the system and about each change?
On each kind of device you ship, which screen readers, control tools and text sizes will you test?

options.l: VoiceOver on Apple, TalkBack on Android phone, Wear and TV, NVDA/JAWS on web [S-L14-080, S-L10-072].
Switch Control, Voice Control, Full Keyboard Access, Dwell Control [S-L14-079, S-L14-007].

questions.ask: In what forms should the system leave the builder: code, a command, files, a pull request, or Figma?

options.l: Copy snippets (Radix "Copy Theme", Utopia CSS) [S-L16-323, S-L16-341].
A one-line install command from a URL (tweakcn via shadcn) [S-L16-333, S-L16-328].
A pull request to the repository [DC-L16-12].
Push to Figma or Paper through MCP [S-L16-002, S-L16-020].
Make the builder's generator an MCP tool that AI can call (Leonardo's example) [S-L16-338].

questions.ask: Where should the docs live, and what should each component's page show?

options.l: Figma plus Storybook (69% and 61% of teams) [S-L11-030].
A docs tool (zeroheight, Supernova), when people who don't code write the docs [S-L11-088].

questions.ask: How should AI coding tools like Claude, ChatGPT, Codex or Cursor read your system?

options.l: An MCP server (Figma MCP at mcp.figma.com; Storybook MCP; shadcn MCP) [S-L11-041, S-L11-044, S-L11-045].
llms.txt and Markdown twins of docs (Cloudscape, Geist) [S-L11-048; L09 A1 row 10].
Rules files for AI agents (from Figma's create_design_system_rules) [S-L11-041].

questions.ask: How should we catch screens that break the system's rules, whether a person or AI made them?

options.l: Lint rules shipped with the tokens, like target size, labels and one main button [DC-L11-24; L13 E3].
Scans that catch raw colors and one-off components (Lovable) [S-L11-053].
Drift detection at the docs layer (zeroheight MCP) [S-L11-104].
Tests that measure how well AI agents follow the system (evals) [S-L11-108].

questions.ask: Should I give tips as you go, stay quiet, or block export on serious problems like contrast?

options.l: Plus a panel that scores how complex and colorful it is [S-L15-047].

questions.ask: When the AI changes your design, how should you review it and try other versions?

options.l: AI changes arrive as patches you review, with before and after views [DC-L16-04].
Your own edits wait, then save all at once (Figma Make) [S-L16-026].
Lock what you like and shuffle the rest, for every setting (shadcn create, Realtime Colors) [S-L16-327, S-L16-335].
A "show 6" grid of versions on the same sample screen [DC-L16-05].

questions.ask: How should the builder handle shapes that look off to the eye, like icon sizes and nested corners?

glossary.plain: The one strong color used for main buttons and for things you pick.
glossary.designer: One accent keeps a calm, focused feel and makes color mean "you can act here". Add a second accent only when it has a job, not for decoration.
glossary.engineer: Roles like color.bg.accent.bold, color.text.accent and color.border.focus alias color.accent.* steps. Accent text passes 4.5:1 and accent boundaries 3:1 in every mode.

glossary.plain: A name that points to another choice instead of holding a value of its own.
glossary.designer: A token that borrows another token's value, so one change flows down the chain. It is how semantic and component tokens stay linked to the palette.
glossary.engineer: DTCG 2025.10: $value "{color.accent.light.9}" targets a whole token; {"$ref": JSON Pointer} reaches inside values. Chains are allowed; circular references are errors. Figma variables alias within one type.

glossary.plain: The small pieces a part is built from, like the box, the words and the icon of a button.
glossary.designer: The numbered parts of a component (container, label, icon) shown in its spec, so designers and engineers use the same names when discussing spacing, color and states.
glossary.engineer: Named parts map to Figma layers or slots and to code sub-elements; planned component tokens name them: button.primary.container.color (proposed). EightShapes generates anatomy diagrams from layers.

glossary.plain: A question that asks if you have something a person must make, like a logo.
glossary.designer: For logo, app icon, icons, illustration, photography, brand type, motion, sound and more, OpenDesigner asks "Do you have this?", lists accepted formats and offers fallbacks; placeholders are always labeled.
glossary.engineer: 19 rows in data/hooks.json (14 asset, 5 tool); asset rows carry ask, accepts, does and if_no. Statuses: have, commissioning, tool, open-library, placeholder, not-needed.
glossary.designer_says: asset request: do you have this?

glossary.plain: A screen width where the page changes its layout, like going to one column on a phone.
glossary.designer: Each one is a moment the layout visibly reorganizes: panes appear, navigation moves from bar to rail. Fewer breakpoints mean bigger shifts; design mobile first.
glossary.engineer: Material 600/840/1200/1600dp width breakpoints (Tailwind's set for web-only), written as rem media queries. DTCG has no breakpoint type, and OpenDesigner does not generate breakpoints yet.

glossary.plain: A row of shades of one color, from very light to very dark.
glossary.designer: Evenly stepped shades of one hue, usually 11 or 12 steps, so backgrounds, borders, hovers and text come from a set, not by eye.
glossary.engineer: Ordered primitives like color.accent.light.1 to .12 plus a dark ramp: 12 steps generated in OKLCH as DTCG color objects with hex fallback; semantic tokens alias into them.
glossary.example: Light blue for backgrounds, dark blue for text on them.

glossary.plain: A ready piece of the screen, like a button, that you can use again and again.
glossary.designer: A reusable part with defined anatomy, variants, sizes and states, styled only by tokens. OpenDesigner's catalog lists 64 canonical components in 10 categories, from Button to App shell.
glossary.engineer: A Figma component with properties (variant, boolean, instance swap, text, slot) mirrored by a code component with props; Code Connect links them. Docs in opendesigner/components/<name>.md are planned.

glossary.plain: A saved value for one part only, like the color of the main button.
glossary.designer: Lets one component be restyled on its own (button.primary.bg) without changing every accent in the product. Add them only when a brand must tune that component separately.
glossary.engineer: Planned tier 3, not generated yet: button.primary.bg (proposed) = "{color.bg.action.primary}" in component.tokens.json, only for components restyled independently or values shared by three or more.

glossary.plain: A score for how much text stands out from what is behind it; higher is easier to read.
glossary.designer: WCAG 2.2 AA: 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text, icons and control borders, 7:1 in high-contrast themes. Test colors as pairs, never alone.
glossary.engineer: engine.py validate checks every foreground and background pair in every mode with no rounding (4.499:1 fails); APCA Lc 75 on body text is reported as an advisory note.
glossary.example: 4.5:1 passes; 4.499:1 fails, because nothing is rounded.

glossary.plain: How round the corners of a box or button are, from sharp to fully round.
glossary.designer: The most varied visible lever across systems, from 0px to pill (median 6px). Radius should grow with component size, and nested corners stay concentric.
glossary.engineer: CSS border-radius from tokens radius.0 to radius.32 (0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32) plus radius.full; the Roundness dial picks radius.control.

glossary.plain: A dark version of the app where each color is picked with care, not flipped.
glossary.designer: Map by role, not by value: each semantic color gets the dark step that keeps its light-mode contrast. Raised surfaces get lighter; accents soften to reduce glare.
glossary.engineer: A resolver context (theme: dark) loading semantic.color.dark.tokens.json: same token names, re-pointed to other ramp steps (Atlassian 700 becomes 400). CSS scope via [data-theme] or prefers-color-scheme.

glossary.plain: How tightly things are packed on the screen, from roomy to tight.
glossary.designer: Dense layouts feel serious and focused and suit tables and dashboards; spacious ones feel calm and open. Density shrinks padding and row heights, never tap targets.
glossary.engineer: A semantic-tier mode axis (semantic.density.compact|comfortable|spacious.tokens.json), separate from breakpoints and color; each step about 4px (Material -1 to -3). size.target.min stays fixed.

glossary.plain: A file in your project that writes down each design choice for people and AI to read.
glossary.designer: The living, readable record of the system. Each section states the decision and its reason, a token table, use and avoid notes and its zoom level.
glossary.engineer: Generated at the project root by engine.py design-md from state.json, tokens and decisions.md, in Google's DESIGN.md format plus nine OpenDesigner sections; never edited as a source.

glossary.plain: The shared rules and parts that make all the screens of an app look and work the same.
glossary.designer: Foundations, tokens, components, patterns and the guidance and governance around them, so every team ships consistent, accessible screens without re-deciding color, type and spacing each time.
glossary.engineer: OpenDesigner: opendesigner/state.json plus generated DTCG 2025.10 tokens, exports and DESIGN.md; component docs and lint rules are planned. Layers: context, principles, foundations, tokens, components, patterns, guardrails, delivery, governance.

glossary.plain: Turning design choices into code that makes the real app look that way.
glossary.designer: The step where decisions become tokens, CSS and components. When code is generated from the same source, what ships matches the design instead of being re-measured from mockups.
glossary.engineer: engine.py export --format css|tailwind|swift|compose|dtcg writes opendesigner/build/. Tokens carry code syntax so Figma binds to variables; Code Connect makes Figma's MCP emit your components.

glossary.plain: A color, size or other choice with a name, kept in one place for the whole app.
glossary.designer: A named decision (brand blue, 16px spacing, 200ms fade) that design files and code both reference, so changing it once restyles every screen and nothing drifts.
glossary.engineer: A DTCG 2025.10 object with a required $value and a $type such as color, dimension or duration, named by dot path (color.bg.accent) and compiled to CSS custom properties.
glossary.example: Atlassian's space.100 token equals 8px.

glossary.plain: A part that needs a real person to make it well, like a logo or photos.
glossary.designer: Only 9 blocks, but the ones people notice first: brand marks, photography, illustration, motifs, custom icons, pictograms, sound, voice and tone. They are supplied or commissioned, never generated as final.
glossary.engineer: Class D, provenance designer-owned in ontology.json (9 of 211 blocks). Its assets open hooks in data/hooks.json (H-logo to H-brandbook), each with formats, fallbacks and a briefed placeholder.

glossary.plain: A shared way to write design choices that both design apps and code can read.
glossary.designer: The open token format Figma, Penpot, Tokens Studio, Style Dictionary and Terrazzo support, so tokens move between tools without retyping. Stable since 28 Oct 2025.
glossary.engineer: Design Tokens Format Module 2025.10 plus Color and Resolver modules (a Final Community Group Report). Files are .tokens.json with $value, $type, $description, $extensions; themes go in .resolver.json.

glossary.plain: How a move speeds up and slows down, like a car that pulls away and then brakes.
glossary.designer: Decelerate curves make entrances feel quick and arriving; accelerate curves get exits out of the way; linear is only for spinners and progress. Keep a small named set.
glossary.engineer: DTCG cubicBezier: four numbers, x values in [0, 1] and y unbounded, so overshoot is allowed; CSS cubic-bezier(). Defaults: standard (0.2, 0, 0, 1), exit (0.3, 0, 1, 1).

glossary.plain: How high a part of the screen seems to float above the part below it.
glossary.designer: Shows stacking order: most products visibly use three levels (resting, raised, overlay). Depending on the depth model it shows as shadow, lighter tone, border or glass.
glossary.engineer: Semantic elevation.raised, .floating and .overlay: DTCG shadow arrays colored {color.shadow.key} and {color.shadow.ambient}, set by the depth model; in dark mode raised surfaces also step lighter.

glossary.plain: A part that can be read from something you already have, like your logo or site.
glossary.designer: Blocks best taken from what exists: your brand book, live product, repo or Figma file. Each value shows where it came from; you accept, adjust or ignore it.
glossary.engineer: Class E, provenance extractable in ontology.json (2 of 211 blocks; many more can be pre-filled). Read at intake; each value carries its reference id, method and confidence.

glossary.plain: Named colors and sizes kept in Figma, a design app, that can switch to dark mode.
glossary.designer: Figma's version of tokens: color, number, string, boolean, timing and easing values in collections with modes, aliasable across collections and scoped to the right property pickers.
glossary.engineer: Modes: 10 per collection on Professional, 20 on Organization. Native DTCG import takes one file per mode (sRGB/HSL colors, px, seconds); composites like typography do not import.

glossary.plain: Big buttons that are close by are faster to hit than small ones far away.
glossary.designer: Size targets generously and put the primary action near the content it acts on. Label key actions with text and icon. Screen-edge targets help mouse users but hurt touch users.
glossary.engineer: T = a + b·log2(2D/w) (Fitts 1954). Encoded as size.target.min, fixed across densities, plus a lint error for targets under 24x24 CSS px.

glossary.plain: The outline that shows which button or box you are on when you use the keyboard.
glossary.designer: Must show on every background: a 2px ring, 2px offset, following the control's corner, in a color with 3:1 contrast. Never remove it.
glossary.engineer: CSS outline on :focus-visible from focus.ring.width, focus.ring.offset and color.border.focus (per mode); radius.focus = radius.control + offset; forced-colors uses Highlight. WCAG 2.4.7 AA.

glossary.plain: How thick or thin the letters are, from very thin to very bold.
glossary.designer: Most systems use two to four weights: 400 body, 500-600 labels, 600-700 headings. Light (300) only at 32px and up. Weight-led hierarchy looks punchy; size-led looks airy.
glossary.engineer: DTCG fontWeight: a number 1-1000 or an alias (thin 100 to black 900, extra-black 950); CSS font-weight. Expression sets type.weightCount 2-4; Energy sets heading weight 600-750.

glossary.plain: The empty space between things lined up in a row, a column or a grid.
glossary.designer: Even spacing between siblings set once on the container, so every list, toolbar and form keeps the same rhythm without per-item margins.
glossary.engineer: CSS gap on flex and grid containers, from semantic dimension tokens like space.inline.sm = "{space.8}" or space.stack.lg. Figma: number variables scoped to gap.

glossary.plain: A part the tool can work out by itself from a few of your answers.
glossary.designer: About three quarters of a system, such as spacing, ramps, most tokens and components, follows from a few inputs and the eight dials. These get sensible defaults you adjust visually.
glossary.engineer: Class G, provenance generatable in ontology.json (156 of 211 blocks): computed by the synthesis/levers.json formulas from raw inputs and dials, or a sourced default. Shown for adjustment.

glossary.plain: We see things that sit close together, or inside the same box, as one group.
glossary.designer: The best-evidenced visual principle, with a strength order: a shared boundary beats proximity, and proximity beats similarity. Keep space within groups clearly smaller than space between them.
glossary.engineer: Enforced by construction: inner spacing tokens resolve below outer ones (innerOuterRatio 2 to 3.5 by density, in the space group's $extensions.opendesigner). Planned critique: flag containers nested over two deep.

glossary.plain: Columns you can't see that help line things up across a page.
glossary.designer: Columns, gutters and margins that align content. 4, 8 and 12 columns suit most products; 16 suits editorial or wide dashboards. Type never hangs into the gutter; containers may.
glossary.engineer: Not generated yet: grid.columns (proposed) as a number, grid.gutter and grid.margin (proposed) as dimensions per breakpoint, driving CSS grid-template-columns: 4, 8, 12 columns; 16-24px gutters.

glossary.plain: The more choices you see, the longer it takes to pick, unless they are in groups or you can search.
glossary.designer: Holds when choices are known and equally likely; newcomers scan lists one by one. Group, label, order and add search, and default one option. Never cut items to satisfy it.
glossary.engineer: RT = a + b·log2(n) (Hick and Hyman 1952). Planned lint: warn on flat, ungrouped lists above roughly 10-12 items with no search, sections or typeahead (threshold inferred).

glossary.plain: A small picture that stands for an action or thing, like a trash can for delete.
glossary.designer: One library, stroke matched to body text weight, corners matched to Roundness. Label key actions; a meaningful icon standing alone needs a text alternative and 3:1 contrast.
glossary.engineer: SVG on the library grid; size.icon.sm/md/lg = 16/20/24px; icon.stroke.sm/md/lg = 1.5/2/2.5px, scaled by size and label weight.

glossary.plain: How close together or far apart the letters in a word sit.
glossary.designer: Zero at body sizes, slightly positive (+0.02-0.05em) for small text and all caps, slightly negative from about 32px so big headlines feel dense and designed.
glossary.engineer: DTCG letterSpacing is a dimension (px or rem only) inside typography, though em is the natural unit; CSS letter-spacing. Figma letter-spacing variables are px, not %.

glossary.plain: How much room each line of text gets from top to bottom, so lines don't crowd.
glossary.designer: Tight (1.1-1.25) makes headings solid; about 1.5 keeps paragraphs easy to follow. Bigger text wants a smaller ratio, longer lines a larger one; snap to 4px.
glossary.engineer: Unitless number in the DTCG typography composite (lineHeight, a multiplier of fontSize); CSS line-height. Default: ratio rounded to the nearest 4px; Carbon ships compact 14/18 beside 14/20.

glossary.plain: A check that runs by itself and flags a mistake, like too many text sizes.
glossary.designer: Accessibility breaks are errors to fix before export; taste rules, such as more than 10 type sizes or bounce above 0.2, are warnings you may waive with a reason.
glossary.engineer: engine.py validate runs deterministic checks and exits 1 on errors; findings cite their rule; waivers sit in state.json. A stylelint config in opendesigner/lint/ is planned (spec 7.12).

glossary.plain: The empty space outside a box that keeps it away from the things next to it.
glossary.designer: Space around an element or page edge. Prefer padding on the parent and gap between siblings; keep margins for page edges and layout sections so spacing stays predictable.
glossary.engineer: CSS margin. Components set no outer margin; space.section.* spaces groups. Material's page margin is 16 compact, 24 above; page-margin tokens like layout.margin.compact (proposed) are not generated.

glossary.plain: A common plug that lets an AI helper use other apps, like Figma.
glossary.designer: Lets your AI assistant read and write in the tools you use: pull a Figma frame, push tokens to Figma variables or Paper, or show a visual picker inside chat.
glossary.engineer: Model Context Protocol (spec 2026-07-28): servers expose tools, resources and prompts over stdio or remote HTTP; the MCP Apps extension renders server HTML in a sandboxed iframe.

glossary.plain: One full set of the saved values, such as the light set or the dark set.
glossary.designer: Swaps every value at once while names stay fixed: light or dark, compact or comfortable, standard or reduced motion. Designs switch mode instead of being redrawn.
glossary.engineer: DTCG keeps modes in the resolver: a context (theme: light or dark) picks one file per mode, such as semantic.color.dark.tokens.json. Figma: a column per mode.

glossary.plain: How long a move on screen lasts, most of the time well under a second.
glossary.designer: Most UI motion runs 100-300ms: short feels snappy, long feels smooth, past about 500ms it drags. Make exits 20-35% shorter than entrances.
glossary.engineer: DTCG duration tokens. At Energy 50: motion.duration.instant 0, micro 100, short 150, medium 250, long 400, extra 700ms; Energy scales medium and longer by 0.8-1.2.

glossary.plain: Making an app look at home on your phone by using the phone's own buttons and letters.
glossary.designer: System fonts and components almost everywhere, brand only in accents, content and voice. Feels at home and inherits OS updates like Liquid Glass, but looks more like other apps.
glossary.engineer: At the low end, Brand presence 0-25 suggests the system font per platform and nativeShare near 1.0; below 50, a native lead platform keeps its own body size.

glossary.plain: The grays for text, backgrounds and lines, at times with a faint hint of color.
glossary.designer: Pure gray reads neutral and tool-like, suiting photo and data apps; a slight tint toward the brand, warm or cool sets the product's temperature.
glossary.engineer: A 12-step ramp per theme: color.neutral.light.1 to .12 and color.neutral.dark.*. Tinted ramps keep OKLCH chroma about 0.01-0.03 mid-ramp, 0-0.008 at the ends.

glossary.plain: A way to write a color by how light it is, how strong it is and which color it is.
glossary.designer: A perceptual color space: blue 600 and green 600 look equally heavy, so ramps stay balanced and hue swaps keep hierarchy. HSL makes yellows wash out and blues go muddy.
glossary.engineer: CSS oklch(L C H), Baseline since May 2023; Tailwind v4 uses it for its whole palette. DTCG color object: colorSpace "oklch", components [L, C, H], optional hex fallback.

glossary.plain: A choice only your team can make, like who the app is for or which devices it runs on.
glossary.designer: Business decisions, not design work: scope, audience, platforms, principles, governance, terminology. OpenDesigner asks them, pre-fills from hints in your repo or references, and never invents an answer.
glossary.engineer: Class I, provenance owner-input in ontology.json (21 of 211 blocks), so business decisions are not misfiled as designer-owned. Class I questions are asked or pre-filled, never invented.

glossary.plain: The empty space inside a box, between its edge and what is in it.
glossary.designer: Inner breathing room of buttons, cards and fields. Keep it smaller than the space between groups so related things read together; parents own spacing, children never add outer margins.
glossary.engineer: CSS padding, fed by semantic inset tokens such as space.inset.md = "{space.12}" (dimension). Density modes shrink insets one scale step; Material uses padding and gap before margins.

glossary.plain: A tried way to put parts together for a common job, like a sign-up form.
glossary.designer: A composition of components plus behavior rules for a recurring task: forms, validation, search and filtering, empty states, onboarding. It encodes when to use it, not only how it looks.
glossary.engineer: 13 patterns (L08 P1 to P13), each listing the catalog components it composes, its key decisions and evidence-backed rules; stored under the pat.* ontology layer.
glossary.designer_says: UX pattern for a recurring task

glossary.plain: The way a phone or computer expects things like menus and going back to work.
glossary.designer: Share what users perceive as the brand (color, type personality, illustration, voice); adopt the platform's version of how the device works: navigation, back, sheets, pickers, text fields, system icons.
glossary.engineer: The behavior.navigationNative param is true at every Brand presence value. Mapping tokens to platform colors, such as color.text.primary to iOS label, is planned; exports emit literal values.

glossary.plain: A raw value with a plain name, like "blue 500", that says what it is, not what it is for.
glossary.designer: The raw palette and scales (blue.500, space.200) with no meaning attached. Designers pick from semantic tokens instead; primitives are the ingredients those tokens point to.
glossary.engineer: Bottom tier: single-valued tokens such as color.accent.light.9 (OKLCH color object) or space.16 (dimension). Values never change per mode; semantic tokens alias them. File: primitives.tokens.json.
glossary.example: blue.500 is a primitive; it knows its color but not its job.

glossary.plain: Showing only what you need now and keeping the rest out of sight until you ask.
glossary.designer: Main options up front, advanced ones behind a clearly labeled trigger such as "More options" or an accordion. Keep it to two levels, and never hide essentials behind hover.
glossary.engineer: Ontology node pat.disclosure; no DTCG type, it composes components. Built from C53 Accordion or disclosure using the WAI-ARIA disclosure pattern, at most two levels deep.

glossary.plain: A setting on your phone or computer that asks apps to move less, for people who get dizzy.
glossary.designer: Keep feedback (color and opacity changes, crossfades) and remove travel: sliding, scaling, parallax and bounce. A good reduced mode still feels polished, not broken.
glossary.engineer: Web @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce); iOS Reduce Motion, Android Remove animations. OpenDesigner's motion mode (motion.reduced.tokens.json): short fades, movement at 0ms, no translate or scale.

glossary.plain: Looking at a site you like to learn how it is built, without copying its name or logo.
glossary.designer: Carries structure and quality, never identity: no name, logo, photos, copy or proprietary fonts. A reference's brand color lends its role and strength, not its hex.
glossary.engineer: The opendesigner-extract skill reads a URL, screenshot, Figma file, repo CSS or brand book; engine.py intake runs the LEVERS formulas backwards to proposed dials, accepted with --set-by reference --source-ref.

glossary.plain: A small file that says which value files to mix for each look, like light or dark.
glossary.designer: The recipe behind themes: it lists the token sets and switches (theme, brand, density) and which one wins, so tools produce every light, dark or brand combination consistently.
glossary.engineer: DTCG Resolver Module 2025.10: version, sets, modifiers with contexts, and resolutionOrder (later entries win). OpenDesigner writes opendesigner.resolver.json; Terrazzo supports resolvers, Style Dictionary v5 does not.

glossary.plain: A value named for its job, like "page background", that points to a raw value below it.
glossary.designer: Named by role, not by look: color.bg.accent, color.text.subtle. Themes, dark mode and rebrands re-point these names, so designs stay correct without touching every screen.
glossary.engineer: Tier 2: $value is a reference, color.bg.accent.bold = "{color.accent.light.9}". Modes live here; each resolver context re-points it (dark: {color.accent.dark.9}).
glossary.example: Page background is white in light mode and near-black in dark.

glossary.plain: A soft dark patch drawn under something to make it look lifted off the page.
glossary.designer: Two layers read realistic: a sharp contact shadow for the edge and a soft blur for distance, tinted neutral rather than pure black. Shadows are decorative, so boundaries need contrast.
glossary.engineer: DTCG shadow: an object or array of {color, offsetX, offsetY, blur, spread, inset}, emitted as CSS box-shadow. Alias color to {color.shadow.key} so dark mode can swap it.

glossary.plain: The first quick pass: a whole but rough design system from a few answers.
glossary.designer: A handful of questions (scope, audience, platforms, brand, color, logo) yield a complete but coarse system you can use right away, then refine area by area.
glossary.engineer: Zoom level 0: the six zoom0 questions in pacing.json; every other decision keeps its auto_default, so the engine still generates a complete token set and DESIGN.md.
glossary.designer_says: quick sketch of the whole system

glossary.plain: A folder of instructions an AI helper reads so it knows how to do one job well.
glossary.designer: A packaged way of working you load into your own AI tool. OpenDesigner ships as skills: install them and your assistant runs the design-system interview and writes the files.
glossary.engineer: Agent Skills format: a folder with SKILL.md (name and description frontmatter) and optional scripts/, references/ and assets/. Loaded by Claude, ChatGPT and Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI and more.

glossary.plain: The one place where you change a value; every other copy is made from it.
glossary.designer: Decide where edits happen first. Whichever side is not the source drifts unless sync is automatic, so Figma becomes a synced view, not a second master.
glossary.engineer: In OpenDesigner, opendesigner/state.json plus the DTCG tokens it generates; DESIGN.md, CSS, Swift, Compose, Figma and Paper are generated views. Code-canonical remains an option for mature systems.

glossary.plain: A short list of gap sizes the whole app picks from, like marks on a ruler.
glossary.designer: A 4px grid with an 8px rhythm, about 15 steps from 0 to 96. Steps differ enough that tight-within, loose-between grouping reads at a glance.
glossary.engineer: Dimension primitives space.0 to space.96 in px, named by value (space.16 = 16px); components use semantic aliases like space.inset.md = "{space.12}", never raw steps.

glossary.plain: Movement that acts like a real spring, coming to rest with maybe a small bounce.
glossary.designer: Defined by stiffness and damping instead of a fixed time, so motion feels natural and keeps its speed when interrupted. Use bounce for spatial hero moments; fades stay critically damped.
glossary.engineer: No DTCG spring type: store dampingRatio and stiffness (M3 standard 0.9 and 700) in $extensions.opendesigner, derive duration and bounce for Apple, and sample into CSS linear() for web.

glossary.plain: How a part looks at a moment, like when you point at it, press it, or it is off.
glossary.designer: Style enabled, hover, focus-visible, pressed, selected, disabled, loading and error. States that carry meaning need 3:1 against neighbors; touch screens have no hover, so never hide essentials there.
glossary.engineer: CSS :hover, :focus-visible, :active, :disabled plus aria-*. Hover and press shift one and two ramp steps (color.bg.accent.bold-hover, bold-pressed); opacity.state.hover covers unknown colors.

glossary.plain: Colors that tell you how things went, like green for good and red for a problem.
glossary.designer: Success, warning, error and info, each with subtle and bold levels. Never rely on color alone: pair with an icon and text, and put dark text on yellow fills.
glossary.engineer: color.bg.<status>.subtle, .bold, .bold-hover; color.text.<status>, color.border.<status>; icons use color.text.<status>. Text 4.5:1, icons and borders 3:1. Color-only meaning: planned lint error.

glossary.plain: A background layer that things sit on, like a card on a page.
glossary.designer: Stacked background levels (sunken, base, raised, overlay) that separate page, cards and popovers. Light mode separates them with subtle tone plus shadow or border; dark mode with lighter tones.
glossary.engineer: Role-named color tokens re-pointed per theme: color.surface.sunken, .base, .raised, .overlay, plus .nav and .tinted. Compare Material 3 surface-container-lowest to -highest and Carbon $layer-01 to 03.

glossary.plain: A ready page plan made from bigger pieces, like a settings page.
glossary.designer: A page-level arrangement of patterns and components that sets content structure before real content arrives. The catalog covers dashboard, list, detail, settings and marketing landing pages.
glossary.engineer: Five templates in L08, each mapped to catalog ids: a dashboard uses C63 app shell, C33 sidebar, C52 cards and C57 table.
glossary.code_name: L08 template mapped to catalog ids

glossary.plain: A named look for the whole app, such as your brand in dark mode.
glossary.designer: A named combination (Brand A, dark, high contrast) applied across the system. Keep brand, color scheme and density as separate axes so combinations need not be drawn by hand.
glossary.engineer: One permutation of DTCG resolver modifiers; outputs multiply (4, 3 and 2 contexts give 24). Keep modifiers orthogonal. CSS export emits one [data-theme] scope per context.

glossary.plain: A part a coder can make with a named tool, with a few things to watch for.
glossary.designer: Blocks an engineer can produce with a named tool, with a caveat: font sourcing, icons, voice drafting and the token pipeline. OpenDesigner recommends the tool and states the catch.
glossary.engineer: Class T, provenance tool-assisted in ontology.json (23 of 211 blocks): OpenDesigner names the tool (Terrazzo, Figma MCP, Code Connect), runs or links it, states the caveat, records the choice.
glossary.code_name: class T, tool named and recorded

glossary.plain: The area you can tap to press a button, which can be bigger than what you see.
glossary.designer: Minimum hit area: 24 by 24 CSS px on web (WCAG 2.2 AA), 44pt on Apple, 48dp on Android. Visuals may shrink with density; hit areas never do.
glossary.engineer: size.target.min, fixed across density modes: 24 CSS px web, 44pt iOS, 48dp Android. engine.py validate errors when a target token falls below its floor.

glossary.plain: The short list of text sizes an app uses, from small labels to big titles.
glossary.designer: Sizes grown from a base by a ratio: 1.125-1.2 feels calm and dense, 1.25 suits product plus marketing, 1.333+ feels editorial. Use three sizes or fewer per view.
glossary.engineer: size(n) = base x ratio^n, rounded to whole pixels; stored as font.size.* dimension primitives. Expression sets type.ratio 1.2/1.25/1.333; Density above 66 caps it at 1.2.
glossary.example: Base 16 at ratio 1.25 gives 16, 20, 25, 31, 39.

glossary.plain: A set of letters that all share one look, like the letters on an iPhone.
glossary.designer: The main personality choice in type: system fonts feel native, open faces like Inter feel neutral, proprietary faces like Plex or Cereal feel brand-led. Check licence and script coverage early.
glossary.engineer: DTCG fontFamily: a string or an array in fallback order, e.g. ["Inter", "system-ui", "sans-serif"]. Emitted as CSS font-family; Figma import accepts a single string only.
glossary.example: SF Pro on Apple devices, Roboto on Android.

glossary.plain: Another look for the same part, like a bold main button and a plain second one.
glossary.designer: Styled versions of one component that signal emphasis or purpose: primary, secondary, tertiary, destructive. Keep one primary per view; a lint warning for more is planned.
glossary.engineer: A Figma variant property plus code prop (variant="primary"), styled by roles like color.bg.action.primary, not yet by button.primary.bg (proposed). Variants multiply with size and state.

glossary.plain: The order your eye sees things on a screen, set by size, boldness, color and place.
glossary.designer: Guide attention by importance: one dominant element, three distinct levels, no more than three type sizes and one primary action per view. If everything looks the same, nothing stands out.
glossary.engineer: Levers: type.ratio from Expression and emphasis.maxPrimaryPerView = 1 (recorded, not checked yet); a warning above 3 type sizes per view is planned. Role tokens stay decoupled from HTML headings.

glossary.plain: The main rule book that helps apps and sites work for people who can't see, hear or move well.
glossary.designer: Version 2.2, level AA, is the usual target: text contrast 4.5:1, non-text contrast 3:1, visible focus, 24 by 24 CSS px minimum targets. AAA is stricter.
glossary.engineer: Criteria OpenDesigner builds in: 1.4.3 and 1.4.11 contrast, 2.4.7 focus visible, 2.5.8 target size (AA), and 2.3.3 animation from interactions (AAA).

glossary.plain: How far one part of your design has come, from a rough sketch to full detail.
glossary.designer: Everyone starts with a sketch of the whole system, then zooms into any area and can stop at any level with something that works. DESIGN.md shows each section's level.
glossary.engineer: Levels 0 sketch, 1 broad, 2 defined, 3 detailed (references/pacing.json). Questions carry a zoom field; a stage asks only those at or below the level being worked.

glossary.plain: Does every making step in one go, then checks the result for problems.
glossary.designer: The one command to run at the end of a step or session. It rebuilds values, exports, guides and preview, then reports any problems.
glossary.engineer: engine.py build runs generate, then validate. Only with no errors (or --force) does it run export --format all, design-md and preview. It exits 1 on errors.
glossary.example: Run build before you show the result to your team.

glossary.plain: Writes two short, easy pages: one about how your app looks, and one about what it is for.
glossary.designer: Produces the readable guide to the system and a separate product brief. Hand-written notes survive only inside keep blocks; the rest is rebuilt from decisions.
glossary.engineer: engine.py design-md [--out DIR] renders DESIGN.md and PRODUCT.md at the project root from state.json, tokens and decisions.md; only <!-- od:keep --> blocks survive regeneration.
glossary.example: Run it after each choice so the guide stays current.

glossary.plain: Copies your design into the forms that websites, phone apps and design tools can read.
glossary.designer: Hands the system to each place it lives: web styles, a Tailwind theme, Figma variables, Paper, iOS and Android code, all from one source.
glossary.engineer: engine.py export --format css|tailwind|figma|paper|swift|compose|dtcg|all writes one subfolder per format in opendesigner/build/, for example css/tokens.css or swift/DesignTokens.swift.
glossary.example: Export to Tailwind for the website and Swift for the iPhone app.

glossary.plain: Notes a problem or idea about this tool, so you can send it to the people who make it.
glossary.designer: Captures gaps, bugs, confusing steps and ideas while you work, ready to send to the project as an issue. Nothing is posted unless you say yes.
glossary.engineer: engine.py feedback "text" --kind gap|bug|confusing|idea (default idea) appends an F-nnn entry to opendesigner/feedback.md and prints a pre-filled GitHub issue link. Nothing is posted.
glossary.example: A question you had to ask twice becomes a confusing note.

glossary.plain: Turns your saved choices into the full list of colors, sizes and spacing your app will use.
glossary.designer: Rebuilds every design value from your decisions, including light and dark, density and reduced motion. Run it after each step that changes values.
glossary.engineer: Writes opendesigner/tokens/: DTCG 2025.10 files per tier and mode (primitives, semantic, semantic.color.light.tokens.json and .dark, density, motion), opendesigner.resolver.json and opendesigner.meta.json.
glossary.example: Change the brand color, then generate to see new shades.

glossary.plain: Starts a new, blank design in your project, with safe first answers already filled in.
glossary.designer: The first step of a session. It opens a system on sourced defaults, so every later choice is a change from a known starting point.
glossary.engineer: engine.py init [--name "Acme"] [--from path] [--force] creates ./opendesigner/state.json from levers.json defaults and opens decisions.md with entry D-0001. Refuses to overwrite without --force.
glossary.example: Type init once, then answer the first question.

glossary.plain: Looks at the sizes in a site or file you like and turns them into first ideas for your design.
glossary.designer: Turns what was measured on a reference, like its corner radii or type sizes, into proposed dial positions. Nothing changes until you accept. Competitor references propose nothing.
glossary.engineer: engine.py intake <measurements.json> [--accept] [--json] fits reference measurements to proposed dials and raw inputs with confidence levels; --accept records each as set --set-by reference --source-ref <ref-id>.
glossary.example: A site with round buttons suggests a high roundness dial.

glossary.plain: Lock keeps a choice safe so no one changes it by mistake, and unlock lets it change again.
glossary.designer: Protects decisions that must not drift, such as brand colors or accessibility floors. Unlocking needs the owner's clear consent, so later sessions cannot quietly restyle them.
glossary.engineer: engine.py lock <path>, engine.py unlock <path>. Sets locked on the answer or dial record, or adds the path to state.json locks; set refuses locked paths without --force.
glossary.example: Lock the brand teal so no one swaps it later.

glossary.plain: Saves your answer to one question in the chat, along with your reason.
glossary.designer: The shortcut for answering an interview question by its id. One answer can also move linked dials, such as corner softness setting roundness.
glossary.engineer: engine.py pick <Q-id> <option-value> --why "reason". Same as set on answers.<Q-id>; mapped answers also set dials or raw inputs (Q-shape-01 subtle sets dials.roundness to 40).
glossary.example: Pick subtle corners for a busy work tool.

glossary.plain: Makes one web page that shows every color, size and shape in your design, with a few sample parts.
glossary.designer: Builds a single specimen page of every value and a few components, light and dark side by side, so you can judge the system by eye.
glossary.engineer: engine.py preview [--open] writes opendesigner/preview.html, a self-contained specimen of every token and a few components in light and dark; --open launches it in the browser.
glossary.example: Open the preview to see buttons and cards in both modes.

glossary.plain: Shows the exact numbers your choices lead to, like a recipe card for the whole look.
glossary.designer: Shows the real dial positions and every value they lead to, such as type ratio or control radius, so the options you are shown use real numbers.
glossary.engineer: engine.py resolve prints JSON: effective dials (explicit, then preset, coupling and macros, clamped 0-100), dialSources, macroConflicts, zoom and every derived param. Read-only; fills template payloads.
glossary.example: Roundness 45 resolves to a real corner size in pixels.

glossary.plain: Saves one choice and the reason you gave, so it is never lost or forgotten.
glossary.designer: Records a single decision with its rationale. Later sessions see what was chosen and why, instead of guessing from the finished look.
glossary.engineer: engine.py set <path> <json-value> --why "reason" [--set-by delegated] [--lock]. Writes state.json and appends a D-nnnn entry to decisions.md; locked paths need unlock or --force.
glossary.example: Set the brand color to teal because it matches the logo.

glossary.plain: Checks your design for problems, like text too faint to read or buttons too small to tap.
glossary.designer: Runs the checks a careful reviewer would: text contrast, target sizes, naming and unused values. Fix every error before showing results; warnings are worth a look.
glossary.engineer: engine.py validate [--json] checks contrast pairs per theme, that every resolver permutation resolves, target floors, DTCG structure and lint. Exits 1 on errors, 0 with warnings; findings cite rules.
glossary.example: Gray text on a gray card fails and must be fixed.

glossary.plain: A button that copies your picks as short lines of text, ready to paste back into the chat.
glossary.designer: Closes the loop between looking and deciding: your pick, an optional note and a lock box become text the model applies exactly, with no retyping.
glossary.engineer: The #copy button in every template writes OD: lines to the clipboard (navigator.clipboard, execCommand fallback); the note field adds --why and the lock checkbox adds OD:lock lines.
glossary.example: Pick soft corners, press the button, paste in chat.

glossary.plain: A list in the design guide of what to do and what to avoid, for people and AI helpers.
glossary.designer: The guide's rules in plain sentences: what the system guarantees, the do's (one primary action per view) and don'ts (never shrink hit areas), plus any waivers.
glossary.engineer: Section 8 of DESIGN.md (## Do's and Don'ts), written by design-md: rules enforced by construction, Do and Don't bullets, current validation findings and waivers with reasons.
glossary.example: Don't use motion as the only signal.

glossary.plain: A short block of settings at the top of the design guide, set out so a computer can read it.
glossary.designer: The machine-readable header of the design guide: main colors, type styles, corner radii, spacing and key components, so other AI tools pick up the look quickly.
glossary.engineer: YAML front matter in DESIGN.md using only Google's DESIGN.md keys (version, name, description, colors, typography, rounded, spacing, components), filled from default-mode semantic tokens. DTCG files stay canonical.
glossary.example: primary: the main brand color as a hex value.

glossary.plain: A short note, added only if you say yes, that tells new AI helpers to read your design rules first.
glossary.designer: Keeps later AI sessions on-system: they read the design guide and values before touching UI, stop hard-coding values, and ask before changing locked decisions.
glossary.engineer: assets/output/AGENTS-snippet.md, appended to AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md after asking: read DESIGN.md, PRODUCT.md and tokens first, never hard-code values, run engine.py review after implementation.
glossary.example: A new AI session reads it before styling a page.

glossary.plain: The folder with ready copies of your design for web pages, phone apps and design tools.
glossary.designer: Where the exports land, one per tool the team uses: web styles, Tailwind theme, Figma import files, Paper, iOS and Android. Rebuilt, never edited by hand.
glossary.engineer: opendesigner/build/, written by engine.py export: css/tokens.css, tailwind/theme.css, figma/variables.json, paper/, swift/DesignTokens.swift, compose/DesignTokens.kt, dtcg/<name>.resolver.json.
glossary.example: Your web app imports the file in css.

glossary.plain: A diary of every choice made, with how it was made, when and why.
glossary.designer: The running history of the system: each decision with its reason, how it was set and whether it is locked. Teammates read it to learn why.
glossary.engineer: opendesigner/decisions.md is append-only, ADR-style. Each set, pick, lock and init adds a D-nnnn entry: path = value, set_by, locked, date, supersedes, source_ref and reason.
glossary.example: D-0002: corners set to subtle because it is a dense tool.

glossary.plain: A list of problems and ideas you found while using this tool, kept so you can send them in later.
glossary.designer: A running list of gaps, bugs, confusing steps and ideas noticed during a session, kept on your machine until you choose to send them to the project.
glossary.engineer: opendesigner/feedback.md, appended by engine.py feedback: one F-nnn entry per note with date, kind and a pre-filled issue link. Stays local; the person submits the issue.
glossary.designer_says: running list of gaps and ideas
glossary.example: F-001: no question about chart colors in dark mode.

glossary.plain: A single web page that lets you see your whole design at once, in light and dark.
glossary.designer: A specimen sheet for judging the system as a whole: colors, type, spacing, corners, depth and sample components, light and dark side by side.
glossary.engineer: opendesigner/preview.html, written by engine.py preview or build: one self-contained HTML file that uses the generated CSS variables to show every token and a few components.
glossary.example: Open it in any browser, with no setup.

glossary.plain: A short page about your product: who it is for, what it does and where it runs.
glossary.designer: The product brief kept apart from the visual system: audience, surfaces, the memorable thing, ranked principles, constraints and scope. It changes at a different pace than the look.
glossary.engineer: PRODUCT.md at the project root, rendered by engine.py design-md from state.json context. Headings: Product, Audience, Surfaces, Memorable Thing, Principles, Constraints, Scope, Team and Governance.
glossary.example: An invoicing app for small shop owners, on web and iPhone.

glossary.plain: A one-page note that tells your team, in plain words, why the design looks the way it does.
glossary.designer: A one-page case for teammates who will not read the log: the five choices that shape everything, what the rules guarantee, and what is still open.
glossary.engineer: opendesigner/RATIONALE.md, written by the model (not the engine) from decisions.md using assets/output/RATIONALE.md; refreshed after each extend session; ids only in footnotes.
glossary.example: We chose soft corners because the app is for families.

glossary.plain: The one file that holds all your answers and settings; everything else is made from it.
glossary.designer: The single record of every answer, dial position, brand input and asset status. Change the system by changing a decision here through the engine, never by editing outputs.
glossary.engineer: opendesigner/state.json (schema opendesigner-state/1): answers {Q-id: {value, set_by, locked, decision}}, dials 0-100, raw inputs, overrides, hooks, locks, zoom, hashes. Tokens and views generate from it.
glossary.example: Your brand color and corner choice both live here.

glossary.plain: The folder that holds the main list of every color, size and timing in your design.
glossary.designer: The source of truth for every design value. Figma, CSS and app code are copies made from it, so a change here reaches all of them.
glossary.engineer: opendesigner/tokens/: canonical DTCG 2025.10 files, one per tier and mode (primitives.tokens.json, semantic.color.dark.tokens.json), plus opendesigner.resolver.json. Written by generate; never hand-edited.
glossary.example: The dark mode colors sit in their own file here.

glossary.plain: Shows where art like your logo stands: you have it, someone is making it, or it is not needed.
glossary.designer: Tracks assets only a person should create, such as logo, icons or photos: have, commissioning a designer, open library, a named tool, placeholder, or not needed.
glossary.engineer: hooks.<H-id>.status in state.json: pending (until asked), have, commissioning, tool, open-library, placeholder or not-needed. Set with engine.py set hooks.H-logo.status '"have"'; other values are rejected.
glossary.example: Logo: commissioning, since a designer is drawing it.

glossary.plain: The step-by-step chat where the AI asks you one big question at a time and saves your answers.
glossary.designer: A guided conversation that starts with a quick sketch of the whole system, then zooms into the areas you care about, one high-impact question per turn.
glossary.engineer: Run by the opendesigner skill: questions from references/stages/, metadata in questions.json, pacing in pacing.json; each answer goes through engine.py pick or set into state.json.
glossary.example: First question: what are you making?

glossary.plain: A short line of text that stands for one choice, which you paste back into the chat.
glossary.designer: The one format every click and reply turns into, so a choice made in a visual picker lands in the record exactly, with an optional reason and lock.
glossary.engineer: A line starting OD: (set, lock, unlock, accept, ignore, remix), such as OD:set Q-shape-01="subtle" --why "dense tool", applied with engine.py set or lock.
glossary.example: OD:set dials.roundness=65 means softer corners (12px).

glossary.plain: A short name tag for each question, so you can go back and change that answer any time.
glossary.designer: The stable handle for a question across sessions. Say "change Q-shape-01" and any later session finds the same decision, its history and what it affects.
glossary.engineer: Format Q-<area>-<nn>, such as Q-shape-01, listed in questions.json. engine.py set turns a bare Q-id into answers.<Q-id>; decisions.md entries carry it.
glossary.example: Q-color-01 is the question about your brand color.

glossary.plain: The answer the AI suggests, with a reason, and it only counts once you say yes.
glossary.designer: Every question comes with one suggested option and a short reason tied to your answers, with sources on request. Accepting it records a confirmed default, not your own choice.
glossary.engineer: Listed first among 2 to 4 options on the question card, with its reason in brackets. Accepting records --set-by confirmed_default; a recommendation is never logged as chosen.
glossary.example: Subtle corners, because your app is a busy work tool.

glossary.plain: A guess put in so the work can go on, marked for you to check later.
glossary.designer: A stand-in answer for something only the owner knows, like audience or brand facts. It keeps work moving but must be confirmed and never shown as decided.
glossary.engineer: set_by: assumed, via --set-by assumed (a leading "pending:" in --why maps here too). DESIGN.md Open Items and the final summary list every assumed path for confirmation.
glossary.example: Audience set to office workers until you confirm.

glossary.plain: A safe answer left in place for you, because no one got to that question.
glossary.designer: A sourced default that stands because the question was never reached, or had one right answer. It goes in the stage summary so someone can revisit it.
glossary.engineer: set_by: auto_default; unreached or mechanical questions need no command. init logs D-0001 this way; auto_default decisions logged with a value appear in DESIGN.md Open Items.
glossary.example: You stopped early, so the icon size kept its default.

glossary.plain: Means you picked this answer yourself.
glossary.designer: The strongest status: the owner made this call. Treat it as intent, and raise any concern as a question rather than changing it.
glossary.engineer: set_by: chosen, the default for engine.py set and pick when --set-by is omitted. Stored on the answer or dial record and in its decisions.md entry.
glossary.example: You typed teal, so teal is chosen.

glossary.plain: We gave you a suggested answer and you said yes to it.
glossary.designer: The owner saw the recommended default and accepted it. It counts as decided, but tells reviewers the idea came from the recommendation.
glossary.engineer: set_by: confirmed_default, recorded with engine.py set <path> <value> --set-by confirmed_default. A leading "default:" in --why is read as this status too.
glossary.example: The suggestion was 16px text, and you said fine.

glossary.plain: You said "you decide", so the AI made this choice for you.
glossary.designer: The owner handed this call to the model. It still carries a reason, and it is listed at the next approval gate so the owner can review it.
glossary.engineer: set_by: delegated, via engine.py set <path> <value> --set-by delegated --why "<model's reason>". Listed at the next gate and in DESIGN.md Open Items.
glossary.example: You said pick any motion, so the AI chose calm motion.

glossary.plain: A choice kept safe, so no one can change it without asking and unlocking it first.
glossary.designer: Use it for what must not drift: brand hexes, accessibility floors, anything the owner fixes. Later sessions have to ask before touching it.
glossary.engineer: A path with locked: true on its answer or dial record, or listed in state.json locks. engine.py set refuses it until it is unlocked, or --force with consent.
glossary.example: The logo color is locked, so a new page cannot change it.

glossary.plain: Taken from a site or file you shared as an example you like.
glossary.designer: The value came from a reference you shared, measured for structure and quality only. Another brand's logo, exact hue or proprietary typeface is not copied.
glossary.engineer: set_by: reference, with --source-ref <ref-id>; written by engine.py intake --accept or set --set-by reference. The ref id points into state.json references.
glossary.example: Tight spacing taken from a site you admire.

glossary.plain: An old choice that a newer one replaced, with both kept in the diary so you can see the change.
glossary.designer: Nothing in the history is erased. When a decision changes, the old entry stays and the new one points back to it, so you can trace how the system grew.
glossary.engineer: decisions.md is append-only: a later entry for the same path supersedes the earlier one and records supersedes: D-nnnn. The newest entry per path is the effective value.
glossary.example: D-0009 replaces D-0002 when corners go from subtle to soft.

glossary.plain: What a screen is for: selling something, getting work done, reading, or enjoying an experience.
glossary.designer: Persuade, Operate, Read or Experience, set for each surface. It changes spacing, card use and big hero moments, not the brand.
glossary.engineer: answers.Q-scope-06 fills context.surfaces with {name, mode}. The main surface sets raw.productType; any Persuade or Experience surface sets raw.marketingSurfaces. No dial moves.
glossary.designer_says: surface mode: persuade, operate, read, experience
glossary.example: A landing page is Persuade; the dashboard behind it is Operate.

glossary.plain: A small web page that shows each option as a real sample, so you can see it before you pick.
glossary.designer: Show, then ask: a live sample of each option on real components (palette, type scale, spacing ruler, radius, elevation, motion, component sheet, option gallery) instead of a description.
glossary.engineer: One of eight self-contained HTML files in assets/templates/, fed a JSON payload in its od-data script and filled from engine.py resolve; show.py opens a local copy.
glossary.example: The radius page shows buttons with four corner sizes.

glossary.plain: How much care a question gets: big choices get more time, and small ones get a quick yes.
glossary.designer: Tells the model where to slow down. High-weight questions shape many others, so they get real options and a line on what else changes; low-weight ones get a quick default.
glossary.engineer: The weight field (high, medium, low) in questions.json: high means fan-out 5+ or a Quick question, medium fan-out 2-4 or owner inputs, low otherwise, per pacing.json.
glossary.example: Brand personality is high weight; icon stroke is low.

glossary.plain: The list of problems the checker found: ones you must fix and ones worth a look, each with its rule.
glossary.designer: Tells you what blocks shipping (errors, like text contrast under 4.5:1 or targets under 24px) and what needs judgment (warnings), each citing its rule and source.
glossary.engineer: Printed by validate or build, or JSON with --json: items with severity (error, warn, info), category, rule, where, measured, threshold, evidence and fix; plus lowest ratios and a summary.
glossary.example: Error: body text on gray is 3.9 to 1, below 4.5.

glossary.plain: The second step of detail, with one quick screen for each main part of your design.
glossary.designer: Zoom level 1: one short screen per foundation (style, density, color use, text, corners, depth, motion, where files live). About 8 questions and 8 minutes.
glossary.engineer: Zoom level 1: the eight questions in pacing.json zoom1. Stored as state.json zoom.<area> = "broad", or inferred from 1-2 decisions in the area.
glossary.example: One screen picks corners, the next picks depth.

glossary.plain: The third step of detail: you pick one part, like color, and set it with real numbers.
glossary.designer: Zoom level 2: one area at a time, such as color ramps, roles and contrast, with real values. Take only the areas that matter for your product.
glossary.engineer: Zoom level 2: an area's level-2 questions in stage order, then engine.py generate. Stored as zoom.<area> = "defined", or inferred from 3-5 decisions in that area.
glossary.example: Zoom into color to set exact shades and contrast.

glossary.plain: The deepest step, where every small part and button is worked out in full.
glossary.designer: Zoom level 3: the fine print of each area plus blocks, components and patterns, built from the system's values rather than from scratch.
glossary.engineer: Zoom level 3: questions tagged zoom 3, from stages/NN-*.detailed.md. Stored as zoom.<area> = "detailed", or inferred from 6 or more decisions or any override in that area.
glossary.example: Every button state, such as hover and disabled, is set.

glossary.plain: A slider for how much the app looks like your brand, or like the phone it runs on.
glossary.designer: Native (0): system font and components, brand only in accents. Brand-led (100): custom face, brand color on large surfaces, custom components. Navigation, back and sheets always stay native.
glossary.engineer: Posture dial, default 50. Sets guidance params type.faceSuggestion, brand color placement, nativeShare (1.0 at 0, 0.8 at 50, 0 at 100) and content.voiceGuidance; behavior.navigationNative stays true.
glossary.example: Fluent's 80/20 guidance: reuse native components most of the time.

glossary.plain: A slider for how much color the app uses, from all gray to bright and bold.
glossary.designer: Low keeps the palette near gray with one accent; high raises accent chroma, adds secondary and tertiary accents from 60 and tints surfaces. Spend strong color on small, meaningful elements.
glossary.engineer: Character dial 0-100, default 50. Accent chroma for color.accent.* (HCT 0, 10, 34, 48, max), scheme variant (monochrome to vibrant) and accent count (1, or 3 from 60).
glossary.example: Material's scheme variants run from Monochrome to Vibrant along this dial.

glossary.plain: A slider for how much fits on one screen, from roomy and calm to tight and packed.
glossary.designer: Spacious (0) reads calm: 16px+ body, 48px controls. Compact (100) reads serious and efficient: 14px body (13 at 90+), 32px controls. Hit areas never shrink.
glossary.engineer: Posture dial 0-100. Drives type.baseSize.web (19-13), size.control.md (48/40/32), size.icon.default (24/20/16) and density context; size.target.min never changes.
glossary.example: GOV.UK's 19px body sits near 0; Polaris's 13px near 90.

glossary.plain: A slider for how much parts seem to lift off the page, from flat to deep.
glossary.designer: Each band is a different model: borders only, ring plus faint shadow, tonal layers, shadow ladder, then glass materials with a solid fallback. Dark mode lifts raised surfaces by lightness.
glossary.engineer: Character dial 0-100, default 40. The elevation model breaks at 15, 35, 55 and 80; light shadow alpha (color.shadow.key) runs 0.08-0.24; dark mode lifts raised surfaces.
glossary.example: GOV.UK uses borders only; Apple's Liquid Glass sits at the deep end.

glossary.plain: A slider for how lively the app feels, from calm to bouncy and bright.
glossary.designer: Calm (0) uses no-overshoot springs, shorter durations (0.8x), lighter headings and recessive navigation; energetic (100) adds bounce, 1.2x longer medium moves, more saturation and heavier headings.
glossary.engineer: Character dial 0-100, default 50. Sets spatial spring damping ratio (1.0-0.6) and stiffness (700-380) in motion.spring.spatial.*, motion.easing.standard and a duration multiplier (0.8-1.2).
glossary.example: Material 3's standard spring damps at 0.9; its expressive one at 0.8.

glossary.plain: A slider for how much the app shows off, from quiet and plain to bold and loud.
glossary.designer: Productive (0) keeps attention on the task; expressive (100) adds emphasis: a bigger type scale, more weights, hero moments, brand-colored chrome, visible containers and motion throughout.
glossary.engineer: Posture dial 0-100, default 50. Drives type.ratio 1.2/1.25/1.333, type.weightCount 2-4, emphasis.heroMoments, layout.containment, brand color role and expressive motion scope (resolve params).
glossary.example: Above 66, Material-style emphasized type is requested; it is not generated yet.

glossary.plain: A slider for how round the corners are, from sharp boxes to soft pill shapes.
glossary.designer: Sets the default control radius and everything derived from it: container and overlay radii, nested radii, focus-ring radius, icon corners and caps. Benchmark median is 6px.
glossary.engineer: Character dial 0-100, default 50. radius.control bands: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16px, full (pill) at 93+. Sets icon corner style and cap shape (resolve params).
glossary.example: Carbon sits at 0px corners; Material 3 uses full pill buttons.

glossary.plain: A slider for how cool and formal or warm and friendly the grays and the wording feel.
glossary.designer: Cool tints neutrals blue (slate) with title case and firmer borders; warm tints them toward stone or taupe, softens borders, uses sentence case and contractions. Brand hue never moves.
glossary.engineer: Character dial 0-100. OKLCH neutral tint (chroma, hue) of color.neutral.*: slate (0.046, 257) at 0, gray at 50, taupe (0.021, 43) at 100; plus border and casing rules.
glossary.designer_says: cool slate to warm taupe neutrals
glossary.example: Cool end: GOV.UK writes "cannot". Warm end: "can't" and "we".

glossary.plain: The facts you gather first: who it is for, where it runs, how the brand feels, and what limits apply.
glossary.designer: The brief behind every visual choice: purpose, audience, platforms, devices, brand personality and hard limits. Settle these first, because they constrain more later decisions than any other input.
glossary.engineer: Step-0 and step-1 inputs in the decision graph, kept in state.json (context.*, raw.*, answers), not tokens. The brand personality card alone constrains 15 later decisions.
glossary.example: A calm banking app for the web, iPhone and Android.

glossary.plain: What the brand brings: how it feels, how it ties to its ads, and how bold the app may be.
glossary.designer: What the brand brings: its personality, how the expressive identity (logo, campaign color, display type) relates to the productive product UI, and how much expression the product allows.
glossary.engineer: Not tokens: answers.Q-brand-01 sliders become macros that offset dials, answers.Q-brand-04 records expressiveness, and raw.marketingSurfaces widens display type. An expressive mode axis is planned.

glossary.plain: How bold the brand may get in the app, and how many showy moments it is allowed.
glossary.designer: How much brand expression the product allows. Default, Material's rule: productive everywhere plus one or two hero moments with expressive type, shape or motion, kept for key interactions.
glossary.engineer: Planned, not generated yet: expressive variants as a mode or parallel set, such as font.display.emphasized (proposed), shape.corner.expressive.* (proposed), motion.spring.expressive.* (proposed), from DC-L06-03.
glossary.example: A bold, springy success screen after payment; calm screens everywhere else.

glossary.plain: Whether the pages that sell the app and the app itself share one set of design rules.
glossary.designer: Whether marketing (expressive) and product (productive) surfaces share one system or run separately. Default: one system, productive by default, expressive opt-in; split only when separate teams own separate surfaces.
glossary.engineer: Planned, not generated yet: a layer mode axis (productive | expressive), not duplicate tokens. Today Energy picks Carbon productive (0-33) or expressive (67+) curves for motion.easing.enter and .exit.

glossary.plain: A few sliders for how the brand feels, like fun or serious, that guide most later choices.
